question: Did people exposed in the past get the outcome more often, judging by existing records?

steps.title: Find records
steps.text: Look for records that already hold exposure and identity for a whole group, such as employment rolls or health databases.

quotes.text: Researchers often use data for purposes for which they were not originally intended, including, for example, official vital statistics that were collected primarily for administrative purposes

steps.title: Start in the past
steps.text: The cohort's starting line lies in the past; the study idea came after the data were collected.

quotes.text: A second usage distinguishes prospective and retrospective cohort studies according to the timing of data collection relative to when the idea for the study was developed

steps.title: Trace outcomes
steps.text: Follow each person forward in the records, from the starting line to the outcome, death, leaving or the end date.

quotes.text: In cohort studies, the investigators follow people over time.

steps.title: Compare rates
steps.text: Compare outcome rates between the exposed and the unexposed, as in any cohort.

quotes.text: Investigators commonly make contrasts between individuals who are exposed and not exposed or among groups of individuals with different categories of exposure.

steps.title: Mind the gaps
steps.text: You get only what someone happened to record; a missing confounder cannot be asked about now. Say what the data were first collected for.

quotes.text: briefly restating the original aims might help readers understand the context of the research and possible limitations in the data.

confounding-indication.text: Confounding by indication occurs when physicians or other health professionals select patients for a specific exposure

measurement-error.text: Information bias occurs when systematic differences in the completeness or the accuracy of data lead to differential misclassification of individuals regarding exposures or outcomes.

immortal-time.text: Eligibility criteria need to be met at that point but not later; study outcomes begin to be counted after that point but not earlier.

limits: Euser et al. (2009), the card's reference, was not read in this task; the steps follow the STROBE explanation instead.
STROBE notes that prospective and retrospective are used in several ways (item 4); this page uses the second, timing-of-data-collection meaning.
